Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin

Threat.value: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger
I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building
I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment

Memory.value: My memories of the frightening event are very clear and detailed.
The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to

Negative Appraisals.value: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened
The world is a dangerous place
My body has been permanently damaged by what happened

vignette: Raúl had always taken pride in being composed, a prosecutor who could sit through grim testimony without flinching, but after the assault that occurred late one winter evening outside his apartment building, that steadiness began to fracture. He had been returning home alone when a man he knew from the neighborhood approached him under the pretense of a friendly exchange, and the betrayal of a familiar face made the attack feel all the more inescapable. In the months that followed, certain moments seized him without warning: being around children on the courthouse steps, where their voices and small bodies seemed to sharpen his dread; a particular coldness on his skin from winter air or air conditioning that carried him straight back to the physical helplessness of that night; and encounters with related people, especially acquaintances who resembled the assailant in face or manner, which could make his stomach turn before he had fully registered why. When those cues hit, the memory did not arrive as a story he could tell from a distance. It came back with almost unbearable clarity, every detail intact — the angle of the streetlight, the pressure of the pavement, the smell of the man’s jacket — and it forced its way into his mind as if the event were happening again in the present tense. What distressed him most was that these intrusions seemed to confirm what he had already come to believe about himself: that he was dirty, contaminated, and somehow permanently damaged, his body no longer fully his own. Once Raúl had settled into the belief that the world was dangerous and that he could not trust his own sense of safety, ordinary details around him started to feel charged with threat, and cues that might once have passed unnoticed — children on the courthouse steps, the bite of cold air, or a familiar man in his peripheral vision — now snagged and held his attention as if they were warnings. Because of that, he began to feel that the world itself was dangerous, and he could not trust even ordinary surroundings not to turn against him. That constant sense of danger kept bringing the assault back into his mind; when he moved through a corridor or crossed a parking lot on high alert, the memory could arrive fully formed, as vivid and immediate as if it were happening again. Raúl started scanning exits the moment he entered any room or building, noticing knives in restaurant kitchens, heavy tools in garages, anything that might be used as a weapon, and he avoided unfamiliar places altogether because he felt unable to assess the danger quickly enough. The more he judged the world as perilous and himself as physically compromised, the more vigilant he became, and that vigilance made the old images easier to catch and harder to shake. A crowded hallway, a child brushing past him in the courthouse, the sudden chill of conditioned air across his forearms — each could pull the memory back in with such force that it again seemed immediate, which in turn flooded him with the conviction that he was unsafe and irrevocably altered. He then redoubled his attention to exits and objects that could harm him, and he became even more sensitive to the same kinds of cues, watching for children, familiar men, and changes in temperature before they could surprise him. Over time this left him more restricted in daily life; he declined invitations to unfamiliar neighborhoods, took longer routes to work, and stayed on edge during routine hearings, all while telling himself that caution was the only thing preventing another violation. At 67, widowed and living alone, he finally sought help when he noticed that even arriving at court in the morning could set off the same rapid cycle of intrusion, dread, and self-disgust, and he was afraid not only that the memories would keep ambushing him, but that he would continue shrinking his life around them.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette shows negative appraisals increasing vigilance and threat, but it does not clearly say those beliefs caused the specific triggers/cues (children, cold air, familiar men) to appear or become activated.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Memory: The vignette shows threat leading to scanning and avoidance, but it does not clearly state that the sense of danger directly brought the traumatic memory back in.
  e.g. "Walking home on high alert, she passed a doorway and the memory was simply there — pulled out of her by the adrenaline, fully formed."
  e.g. "The persistent sense of danger kept her close to the event in her mind, as if she needed to keep reviewing it to stay one step ahead of whatever came next."
  e.g. "On nights when the threat felt highest, the memory was hardest to keep at bay — it would surface in the dark, vivid and unwelcome."
